steps.observation: Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here are the key differences between DNA and RNA:

1. Sugar backbone  
   • DNA uses deoxyribose (lacking one oxygen atom)  
   • RNA uses ribose (has one extra oxygen)

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA’s four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C), guanine (G)  
   • RNA’s four bases: adenine (A), uracil (U) replaces thymine, cytosine (C), guanine (G)

3. Strand structure  
   • DNA is typically double-stranded, forming a stable double helix  
   • RNA is usually single-stranded and can fold into complex 3D shapes

4. Function  
   • DNA stores and transmits hereditary information in the nucleus (and in mitochondria/chloroplasts)  
   • RNA plays several roles:  
     – messenger RNA (mRNA): carries genetic code from DNA to ribosomes  
     – transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA): help assemble proteins  
     – other regulatory and catalytic RNAs (e.g., microRNA, ribozymes)

5. Stability and lifespan  
   • DNA is more chemically stable (the missing oxygen on deoxyribose makes it less prone to hydrolysis)  
   • RNA is less stable, often short-lived, which suits its roles in transient information transfer and regulation

6. Cellular location  
   • In eukaryotes, DNA resides mainly in the nucleus (also in mitochondria/chloroplasts)  
   • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions largely in the cytoplasm (ribosomes, spliceosomes, etc.)

Summary  
DNA is the long-term, double-stranded genetic blueprint built on deoxyribose and uses thymine, while RNA is a shorter-lived, single-stranded molecule built on ribose and uses uracil, serving as messenger, adapter, structural and regulatory roles in gene expression.
